results.summary_before: This analog design is an 8-bit binary-search analog-to-digital converter intended to digitize analog pixel signals for a CCDmos3D pixel. It generates its own test input signal, feeds it through the ADC, converts the digital result back with a DAC, and outputs both the original and reconstructed signals on two analog pins for comparison. Testing requires a power source for the chip and an oscilloscope to verify that the two analog outputs match. The design is notable for including a self-test path that exercises the ADC and DAC together.

results.summary_before: This controller streams 8-bit PCM audio stored in an external QSPI flash device and reproduces it through a high-frequency PWM output on one of the dedicated and bidirectional pins. After reset it issues a software reset to put the flash into 1-bit mode, then reads data in 8-byte chunks using the Fast Read Quad I/O instruction and buffers them for playback. Two input pins select playback speed among 0.5x, 1x, 1.5x and 2x by repeating or skipping samples. It requires a W25Qxx-style QSPI flash and the Tiny Tapeout audio Pmod, and the clock is only 50 kHz.

results.summary_before: This Verilog controller generates selectable 8-bit digital control patterns for a programmable 4x4 metasurface array used in beam steering. Two input bits select one of four beam-control modes, each producing a different pattern on the eight outputs. It is intended as a demonstration of the digital control principles used when configuring programmable antenna and metasurface elements. Physical testing needs two switches on the mode inputs and eight current-limited LEDs on the outputs, while simulation uses a cocotb testbench that checks all four mode selections.

results.summary_before: This project implements a textbook RSA encryption core that computes message^5 mod 221 using a pipelined square-and-multiply modular exponentiation algorithm. It uses an 8-bit datapath and a shift-and-add multiplier to fit in a 1x1 tile, taking up to 512 clock cycles per encryption. The design is for educational purposes only and is not secure. It requires no external hardware beyond input and output pins.

results.summary_before: This is an 8-bit differential SAR ADC designed as the core for a future noise-shaping SAR ADC. It uses a capacitive DAC and dynamic comparator, with a digital controller that provides timing for sampling and successive approximation. The fabricated version implements only the fundamental SAR conversion, with noise-shaping and DEM reserved for future work. It requires external reference voltages, a bias current, and a 96 kHz clock.
